first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this because her fiance's family is Korean. The opening sets it out as a sequence of steps, which is how my mind works. Calm, no slang, short paragraphs on the iPad. Plenty of new words, but I kept going.

journey.quote: It is a sequence: a gift box carried to the bride's family, gifts passed between two households, a ceremony, then a quieter room where the couple bow to the groom's family and try to catch a skirtful of dried fruit.
journey.reaction: So both households are involved from the start, including ours. Good to know before anything lands on my doorstep.

journey.quote: Gifts such as the ham, yedan, yemul and chukuigeum are settled between families, so agree what you will keep before any amounts are discussed.
journey.reaction: Sensible. Agree the shape before the money. That's exactly the order I'd want.

journey.section: 2. Yedan and yemul: gifts between the two families
journey.quote: Yedan are the gifts the bride's side gives to the groom's family before the wedding. In many families they include bedding, fine clothing or other household gifts for the groom's parents and close relatives.
journey.reaction: That's us. The bride's side. I'd like some idea of what's usual so I don't over- or under-do it, and whether it's polite for me to ask the other mother directly.

journey.section: 4. The jeontong honrye: a traditional Korean wedding ceremony, step by step
journey.quote: The bride's robes are heavy and attendants guide her movements, so allow time in the run sheet.
journey.reaction: Practical. I like that someone has thought about how long things actually take.

journey.section: 6. Korean wedding hanbok: wonsam or hwarot and samogwandae
journey.quote: One example, made in Korea between about 1850 and 1950, has a green body, red ribbons and sleeves striped in red, yellow, blue, white and dark red.
journey.reaction: Lovely, but museum detail is more than I need. I skimmed to find out whether the bride's mother is meant to wear hanbok too.

journey.section: 7. The pyebaek, or paebaek: bows to the groom's family
journey.quote: Many families now include the bride's parents as well.
journey.reaction: Oh. So I might be sitting behind that low table. On floor cushions? My knees, and my mother's walking frame. I'd need to know whether chairs are acceptable.

journey.section: 9. Chukuigeum: the gift envelope at the reception desk
journey.quote: Each family usually staffs its own desk, and amounts are never discussed openly.
journey.reaction: So our side looks after a desk full of cash envelopes. Who on our side does that, and where does the money go afterwards? Glad I read it here first.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise normal safety precautions in South Korea", with no higher-level areas.
journey.reaction: Good, that's the first thing my husband would check, and it's dated. The weather months are useful too.

journey.section: Seoul and Jeju as places couples choose
journey.quote: Couples who marry in South Korea often choose Seoul, close to family, hotels and the city's wedding halls, or Jeju, the island to the south, for a smaller gathering by the sea.
journey.reaction: Fine, but nothing about getting older relatives there: the flight, transfers, steps, medical care, travel insurance. That's what I'd actually worry about.

journey.section: Legal paperwork: certificates and district office registration
journey.quote: Read [Getting married overseas](https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/planning-trip/advice-your-planned-activities/getting-married-overseas) and talk to a lawyer to confirm your marriage will be valid.
journey.reaction: Honest. It tells me who to ask rather than pretending to be the lawyer. The question list for the district office is the sort of thing I'd print out.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia
journey.quote: Who will source the table, the screen and the hanbok, and who will set them up?
journey.reaction: Exactly my kind of question. Someone has thought about who does what.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia
journey.quote: They work in your time zone and quote in AUD, the fee is agreed in writing before any work begins, and your advisor confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: That's the sentence I was looking for. Australian dollars, in writing, before anything starts. It still doesn't say what happens to deposits paid to a hotel in Seoul, or who I ring if something goes wrong at 2am Korean time.

journey.section: Holding a pyebaek at home in Australia
journey.quote: The legal marriage, any registration and every family custom stay with you, your families and your celebrant.
journey.reaction: Clear about who's responsible for what. I respect that.

journey.section: Planning your Korean wedding with us
journey.quote: You will meet one Wedded Advisor, your single point of contact from the first call to the wedding day.
journey.reaction: One person and a first call. That's what I want. I'd like to know that call happens before anything is booked.

unanswered_questions: As the bride's side, what yedan is usually expected, and is it all right for me to ask the groom's mother directly?
If the bride's parents join the pyebaek, can older family sit on chairs rather than floor cushions?
What should a non-Korean mother of the bride wear, and would hanbok be welcome or awkward?
Who on our side looks after the chukuigeum envelopes, and how is the money kept safe?
If the wedding is in Seoul or Jeju, can an elderly guest with a walking frame manage the flights, transfers and venues, and what travel insurance and medical cover should she have?
If we pay deposits to a hotel or hall in Korea, is that money protected, and are contracts in English and AUD?
Who do I ring if something goes wrong on the day in Korea? Is anyone from your side there?
Can I speak with the Wedded Advisor by phone before anything is booked?
would_share_with: My husband, with the Smartraveller line, the legal paperwork questions and the fee-in-writing sentence marked
My daughter, to ask what yedan our side should give and whether Nana can manage the pyebaek and a trip to Korea

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready to talk through dates, places or a pyebaek at home, tell us your date, your guest list and the feeling you want. Nothing is too early or too vague.
cta_reaction.why: 'Nothing is too early or too vague' is kind, and the fee in writing plus one named contact help a great deal. But I want to know a real person will ring me before anything is booked, and how deposits overseas are handled.

top_3_changes: In the yedan section, add a line for the bride's family on how to open the gift conversation with the groom's family (as questions to ask, no invented amounts).
In the Seoul and Jeju or pyebaek section, add a short note for older or less mobile relatives (seating at the pyebaek, transfers, medical cover, travel insurance), framed as questions to ask.
At the closing invitation, say plainly that it starts with a phone call with a named person, and list deposits and on-the-day support as questions to raise on that call.

open_questions.question: Deposit protection for Korean venues, on-the-day support and accessibility for elderly guests remain this persona's main trust gaps, but business details are deferred. Treat as nice-to-have or route to CRO for the CTA block?

Per orchestrator, brand voice does not discuss sourcing; the museum-detail comment is a readability point, not a request for sourcing commentary.
